title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 112: The Terracotta Army of Xi'an
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 112 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Terracotta Army of Xi'an

Paragraph 1. In March 1974, during a severe drought in Shaanxi province, northern China, a group of farmers began digging a water well east of Mount Li. Several metres down, their shovels hit baked clay, followed by life-sized terracotta heads and bronze spear tips. Without realising it, the farmers had found the outer edge of the massive burial complex built for Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor, who died in 210 BCE.

Paragraph 2. Archaeological excavations later uncovered an enormous underground complex covering roughly 56 square kilometres across four main pits. Pit 1, the largest hall, contains an estimated 6,000 clay soldiers alongside forty wooden chariots, arranged in military rows facing eastward against potential spiritual attacks from rival states. The figures display distinct military roles, from kneeling archers to commanding generals.

Paragraph 3. Building this vast clay army required smart industrial organisation. Workers baked local clay in huge underground ovens above 900 degrees Celsius. To keep the heavy statues balanced, builders made solid clay legs, while upper bodies and heads were constructed hollow. Rather than making identical copies from a single face mould, sculptors carved individual ears, mustaches, hairstyles, and expressions by hand so no two soldiers looked alike. To enforce strict quality, each master worker stamped his personal name into the wet clay before firing.

Paragraph 4. Although modern visitors see monotone grey statues, every warrior originally wore brilliant colours: red, green, blue, and synthetic Han purple. Sadly, the figures had lain in wet earth for two thousand years. When dug out into dry air, the underlying lacquer dried out in seconds, destroying the bright paint within four minutes. Consequently, major digging paused until scientists developed special moisture-saving sprays.

Paragraph 5. The warriors were armed with real bronze weapons, including arrows and double-edged swords, which remained amazingly sharp and rust-free. Early researchers guessed Qin craftsmen had coated blades with anti-rust chromium, but modern scanning tests disproved this idea: tiny chromium traces simply came from tree varnish on nearby wooden cases. Instead, the weapons survived thanks to the surrounding earth, whose alkaline chemistry and tightly packed clay blocked air and water.

groups.title: Questions 6–10
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN.

steps: Đoạn 1: "...during a severe drought in Shaanxi province..."
Đoạn 3: "...stamped his personal name into the wet clay..."
Đoạn 4: "...the underlying lacquer dried out in seconds..."
Đoạn 5: "...whose alkaline chemistry and tightly packed clay..."

q6.text: Pit 1 holds more wooden chariots than human terracotta soldiers.

steps: Đoạn 2: Hầm 1 có khoảng 6.000 lính và chỉ 40 chiến xa gỗ.

q7.text: No two excavated terracotta warriors look completely identical.

q8.text: Excavations continued smoothly without stopping even when paint peeled off.

steps: Đoạn 4: Việc khai quật lớn phải tạm dừng (major digging paused) để chờ công nghệ giữ ẩm.

q9.text: Modern lab scans confirmed that Qin workers intentionally plated swords with chromium.

steps: Đoạn 5: Các thử nghiệm hiện đại đã bác bỏ giả thuyết này (disproved this idea).

q10.text: Several terracotta statues were damaged while being transported to foreign museums.

steps: Đoạn 4 & 5: Không hề nhắc việc tượng bị hư hại khi vận chuyển đi bảo tàng nước ngoài.
